chunks: And from him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from his brother Al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said:

I asked him about a man who catches the Maghrib prayer while on the road; should he delay it until the twilight disappears? He said, 'There is no harm in that during travel, but as for being at home, it is slightly less than that.'

So all these narrations indicate that these times are for the one with an excuse, because they are restricted by impediments and what follows their pattern. And that which reveals what we mentioned is that delaying Maghrib - from the disappearance of the sun - is not permissible except for an excuse. Whatever is established that he is commanded to pray at this time, the command for us is upon immediacy, so it must be that the prayer is obligatory upon him in this state, and it also indicates this.
ai.seo_question: When is it permissible to delay the Maghrib prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib* clarifies the distinction between *fawr* (immediacy) and permissible delay (*ta'khir*) in Maghrib prayer, noting that while travelers may delay until the disappearance of twilight, residents are expected to pray slightly earlier. The commentary emphasizes that these flexible timings apply specifically to those with valid excuses (*awdar*), reinforcing the Shia principle that the default command for prayer is immediate performance unless an impediment justifies postponement.
